meta.title: Who really said "Some people believe football is a matter of life and death. I can assure you it is much, much more important than that"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Shankly never said it in those words. Granada TV, 1981: "it's more important than that" — and the joke was already credited to UCLA's Red Sanders.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Some people believe football is a matter of life and death. I can assure you it is much, much more important than that'?
meta.ogDescription: Shankly made the joke, but not in this sentence — and American papers were crediting UCLA coach Red Sanders with it years earlier.

answer.label: Not in these words — a smoothed-out paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: Shankly really did make the joke, but not in this sentence. On Granada Television on 20 May 1981 he told it as an anecdote — “Somebody said that football’s a matter of life and death to you. I said, ‘Listen, it’s more important than that’” — and Oxford Essential Quotations cites an earlier printed version reading “much more serious than that” in the Guardian of 24 December 1973. The popular wording, with “Some people believe” and “much, much more important,” matches neither; and the gag itself was already in American newspapers credited to UCLA coach Red Sanders.

source.excerpt: Yeah, I regret it very much. … Somebody said that football’s a matter of life and death to you. I said, “Listen, it’s more important than that.”
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section gives the wording as “Someone said to me ‘To you football is a matter of life or death!’ and I said ‘Listen, it’s more important than that’,” citing an interview on a Granada Television chat-show hosted by Shelley Rohde on Wednesday 20 May 1981 (Wikiquote ↗).

A different wording appears in print earlier: Oxford Essential Quotations (5th ed., ed. Susan Ratcliffe) gives “Some people think football is a matter of life and death…I can assure them it is much more serious than that,” citing the Guardian of 24 December 1973 — while he was still Liverpool manager (Oxford Reference ↗).

Barry Popik traces the joke to UCLA coach Red Sanders, with print citations crediting Sanders from at least 1966 — the Chicago Tribune of 19 November 1966 has him saying “this game is not a matter of life or death. It’s more important than that” (Barry Popik ↗).
The polished version that circulates today is printed on Liverpool FC’s own site with no source given (liverpoolfc.com ↗), and Wikipedia notes the line is frequently paraphrased (Wikipedia ↗).
source.excerptNote: Shankly’s reply after saying he had put his “heart and soul” into football “to the extent that [his] family suffered,” when Shelley Rohde asked whether he regretted that devotion (Wikipedia ↗).
source.rightsHolder: Granada Television (the 1981 broadcast) and Guardian News and Media (the 1973 report)
source.rightsNote: Both documented sources are modern and firmly in copyright: a 1981 Granada Television broadcast and a Guardian report of 24 December 1973. The popular wording quoted at the top of this page has no identified source at all, so no public-domain status can be claimed for it either — treat the excerpt as a short quotation from copyrighted material.

author.name: Bill Shankly
author.kicker: The man who said something like it
author.heading: Who Bill Shankly was
author.metaLine: 1913–1981 · Scottish footballer and manager of Liverpool, 1959–1974
author.bio: Shankly played for Carlisle United and Preston North End, then managed Carlisle, Grimsby Town, Workington and Huddersfield Town before taking charge of Liverpool in 1959, where he stayed until 1974. He was relentlessly quotable, and the quotability is part of the problem: his most famous line is, as Wikipedia puts it, frequently paraphrased, which is how a wry aside on a chat show hardened into a slogan he never quite uttered. He died on 29 September 1981, months after giving the interview the line is usually traced to.

misattribution.heading: How the sentence got its shape
misattribution.intro: Nobody is inventing a Shankly quote out of nothing here — he told this joke, repeatedly, and it is genuinely his signature line. What has drifted is the wording, and what has been forgotten is that he was returning a remark somebody else made to him, in a gag that was already doing the rounds in American sport.

items.why: The circulating sentence — often extended with “I am very disappointed with that attitude” — is the version Liverpool FC’s own site prints, with no source attached (liverpoolfc.com ↗). It matches neither documented version: not Wikiquote’s sourced 1981 wording, nor the Guardian wording OUP cites, which ends “much more serious than that” (Oxford Essential Quotations ↗).

Barry Popik credits the saying to the UCLA coach Red Sanders (1905–1958), who supposedly aimed it at rival USC in 1949, and records citations crediting Sanders in print from at least 1966 — adding that Shankly’s recorded uses of the saying are much later than 1966 (Barry Popik ↗).

items.scope: Another name it has been pinned on
items.why: Popik logs the Oxford Dictionary of American Quotations (2006) filing a national-championship version — “When you’re playing for the national championship, it’s not a matter of life and death. It’s more important than that” — under the Michigan State coach Duffy Daugherty, marked “attributed” (Barry Popik ↗).

items.scope: A later user of the same gag
items.tag: Later user, not a false credit
items.why: Nobody has pinned the football line on him: Sports Illustrated of 19 September 1977 quotes the basketball coach Lee Rose making his own version of the joke, in his own voice — “I would like to deny the statement that I think basketball is a matter of life and death. I feel it’s much more important than that” — which shows how far the gag had travelled by the late 1970s (Barry Popik ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Shankly’s documented line is “Somebody said that football’s a matter of life and death to you. I said, ‘Listen, it’s more important than that’” — Granada Television, 20 May 1981 (Wikipedia ↗). The polished “much, much more important” sentence is a later tidy-up of a joke he was already passing along.

context.heading: It was an answer about regret, not a boast
lead: The sentence is quoted as swagger — a manager planting a flag for football over everything else. The exchange it comes from is the opposite in tone. Wikipedia’s account of the 20 May 1981 Granada interview has Shankly saying he put his “heart and soul” into football “to the extent that [his] family suffered”; when Shelley Rohde asked whether he regretted that, he answered “Yeah, I regret it very much” and then told the life-and-death story (Wikipedia ↗).

The other thing the popular version hides is that Shankly was relaying a line, not coining one. In his telling, somebody else says football is a matter of life and death to him; his contribution is the comeback. Barry Popik’s research shows the same comeback circulating in American sportswriting years earlier, credited to a college coach (Barry Popik ↗).
context.detailsSummary: The American ancestry of the joke
detailsBody: Popik’s earliest transcriptions are both from 1966: the Los Angeles Times of 5 November 1966 recalls “an old Red Sanders line” — “It’s not a matter of life or death…It’s more important” — and the Chicago Tribune of 19 November 1966 has Sanders saying “this game is not a matter of life or death. It’s more important than that” (Barry Popik ↗).

The joke kept travelling. Sports Illustrated of 19 September 1977 quotes basketball coach Lee Rose saying he would like to deny that he thinks basketball is a matter of life and death: “I feel it’s much more important than that.” The Oxford Dictionary of American Quotations (2006) files a version under Duffy Daugherty, marked “attributed” (Barry Popik ↗).
context.pull: He said it while answering a question about what he regretted.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced Quotes section gives the wording "Someone said to me 'To you football is a matter of life or death!' and I said 'Listen, it's more important than that'." cited to an interview on a Granada Television chat-show hosted by Shelley Rohde on Wednesday 20 May 1981; the page's Disputed section covers only the "Aim for the sky" line, not this one; Shankly's dates are given as 2 September 1913 – 29 September 1981.

Oxford Essential Quotations (5 ed.), edited by Susan Ratcliffe, Oxford University Press, published online 2017, gives the Bill Shankly (1913–81) entry "Some people think football is a matter of life and death…I can assure them it is much more serious than that." with the citation "in Guardian 24 December 1973".

Barry Popik credits the saying to Henry Russell "Red" Sanders (1905-1958), UCLA coach, who supposedly said it about rival USC in 1949, notes citations crediting Sanders in print from at least 1966, states that Shankly also used the saying but that his recorded uses are much later than 1966, and transcribes the Los Angeles Times (5 Nov 1966), Chicago Tribune (19 Nov 1966), Sports Illustrated (19 Sept 1977, Lee Rose) and Oxford Dictionary of American Quotations (2006, Duffy Daugherty, attributed) citations.

Wikipedia states his most famous quotation is frequently paraphrased, and that in a May 1981 interview with Granada Television presenter Shelley Rohde Shankly said he had put his "heart and soul" into football "to the extent that [his] family suffered"; asked whether he regretted that devotion he replied "Yeah, I regret it very much", before adding "Somebody said that football's a matter of life and death to you. I said, 'Listen, it's more important than that.'" It cites the interview as Granada Television, 20 May 1981, via the YouTube URL watch?v=xodsnEQC-H0, and gives Shankly's dates as 2 September 1913 – 29 September 1981 with Liverpool 1959–74 and earlier posts at Carlisle, Grimsby, Workington and Huddersfield.

Liverpool FC's official page prints the quote as "Some people believe football is a matter of life and death, I am very disappointed with that attitude. I can assure you it is much, much more important than that." with no date or source attribution given.

Henry Russell "Red" Sanders (May 7, 1905 – August 14, 1958) coached at Vanderbilt (1940–1942, 1946–1948) and UCLA (1949–1957), and is quoted regarding the UCLA–USC rivalry as saying "Beating 'SC is not a matter of life or death, it's more important than that."

This is the video titled "Life And Death" that Wikipedia cites as its audiovisual source for Shankly's remarks in the 1981 Granada Television interview; the URL resolves and the title was confirmed via YouTube's oEmbed metadata.
